arc_intro: The mystery is solved. Four layers are secured. Ravi greenlights two projects that had been on hold: a real CI/CD pipeline connecting FoodQuick's dev and prod AWS accounts, and a new external logistics vendor integration. After everything you just uncovered, nobody wants to build new trust the sloppy way. This time, every new connection gets built carefully from day one.

tasks.scenario: Ravi kicks off the meeting: 'Before Vikram's mess, I would have just said go build the pipeline, we'll clean it up later if there's a problem. Not anymore. What's different about how we approach this now?'
tasks.question: What should actually be different this time, based on everything found in this investigation?
options: A) Nothing structural — just be more careful and remember to double-check things

B) Every new permission or trust relationship gets scoped correctly and documented from the moment it's created, not granted broadly with a plan to 'fix it later' — because 'later' is exactly how Vikram's leftover access sat unnoticed for 8 months
C) Avoid building any new integrations at all, since they're inherently risky
D) Only Ravi personally should be allowed to create any new IAM roles going forward
tasks.explanation: 'Remember to be careful' — is not a process, Vikram case- fail. Scope correctly, document, do — 'fix it later' without.
tasks.ren_correct: Exactly the right takeaway from everything you just found.
tasks.ren_wrong: Not quite — revisit the core idea: who can do what, and can we prove it?

tasks.question: Quick refresher before building the new pipeline: what does a Role's Trust Policy control?
options: A) What actions the role can perform once assumed
B) Who or what is allowed to assume the role in the first place
C) How long credentials stay valid
D) Which region the role works in
tasks.explanation: Correct answer: Who or what is allowed to assume the role in the first place
tasks.ren_wrong: Not quite — Permission Policy. Trust Policy = who can enter.

tasks.question: A Role's temporary credentials — does anyone need to manually refresh them?
options: B) No — AWS STS automatically issues fresh credentials before the old ones expire
C) Yes, the instance needs a reboot
D) No, but they never expire at all
tasks.explanation: STS automatic- handle do. Manual refresh, reboot.
tasks.ren_wrong: Not quite — revisit the core idea: who can do what, and can we prove it?

tasks.scenario: karthik-dev starts on a new EC2-based image-processing service that needs to read raw images from one S3 bucket and write processed thumbnails to another.
tasks.question: Design his role setup correctly, scoped from the start — no 'will tighten it later.'
expected_answer_contains: IAM Role attached via instance profile, not access keys
Trust policy allows only EC2 as the trusted service
Permission policy scoped to exactly two actions on exactly two specific bucket ARNs — s3:GetObject on the source bucket, s3:PutObject on the destination bucket — nothing broader
tasks.explanation: Apply least privilege and keep a clear audit trail — that is the FoodQuick standard for FQ-142.

tasks.scenario: priya-dev deploys a new Lambda function meant to publish an SNS alert whenever a large order is placed. The role is attached, the function deploys cleanly, but the alert never arrives.
tasks.error_shown:
[ERROR] 2026-07-24T10:03:41Z
AccessDeniedException: User: arn:aws:sts::123456789012:assumed-role/foodquick-order-alert-role/LargeOrderNotifier is not authorized to perform: sns:Publish on resource: arn:aws:sns:ap-south-1:123456789012:foodquick-oncall-alerts because no identity-based policy allows the sns:Publish action
tasks.diagnosis: The role exists and is correctly attached — but its policy only includes the default CloudWatch Logs write permission from the Lambda template. Nobody added sns:Publish when the function's real requirement (sending notifications) was defined.
tasks.fix: Add sns:Publish scoped to the specific topic ARN — not sns:* on all topics.
tasks.explanation: Apply least privilege and keep a clear audit trail — that is the FoodQuick standard for FQ-142.

tasks.scenario: Now the real project: the dev-to-prod CI/CD pipeline. karthik-dev drafts the trust policy for the prod-side deploy role. Given everything from this investigation, review it carefully before it goes anywhere near production.
what_to_find: Principal correctly restricts which account can attempt to assume this role — but that alone isn't enough
No Condition block, no ExternalId — missing the extra layer that prevents a 'confused deputy' scenario
Given everything just learned about how single missing safeguards compound into real incidents, this gap should not ship as-is
tasks.explanation: Map every finding before you change anything — missing one leaves a hole in the investigation.

tasks.scenario: The second project: an external logistics vendor needs read-only access to one S3 bucket of delivery manifests. The vendor has their own separate AWS account.
tasks.question: Design the access approach, and explain what you would have missed before this investigation but won't miss now.
options: A) Share an IAM user's access keys with the vendor over email

B) Cross-account IAM Role, trust policy scoped to the vendor's account with an ExternalId condition, permission policy scoped to read-only on exactly one bucket — and this time, a calendar reminder to review this access at the contract renewal date
C) Make the bucket public since it's just delivery manifests
D) Give the vendor a permanent set of root-equivalent credentials for convenience
tasks.explanation: Cross-account role, ExternalId, scoped to one bucket — technically correct. extra step: calendar reminder to review — Vikram case- 'review do ' root cause.
tasks.ren_correct: The calendar reminder detail — that's the investigation talking. Good instinct.
tasks.ren_wrong: Not quite — risky options. Cross-account role + ExternalId + review reminder — This is correct, complete approach.

tasks.scenario: Before closing this piece, run one more check — habit now — on every role created in this session, checking specifically for anything that resembles the pattern found in Vikram's case.

This is itself worth confirming explicitly rather than assuming, given the investigation this session followed

tasks.scenario: Three more integration requests come in this week. Decide the correct trust pattern for each.

cases.case_1: FoodQuick's data pipeline, running as tasks on ECS containers (ECS runs each container workload as a 'task'), needs S3 and DynamoDB access.
cases.case_2: A third-party analytics SaaS tool, hosted entirely outside AWS, needs read-only access to order data.
cases.case_3: FoodQuick's own mobile backend, on EC2, needs to send push notifications via SNS.

correct_answers.case_1: A Role the service assumes — on ECS that's a Task Role, scoped per-task so the container gets exactly what it needs. Same 'service assumes a Role, never static keys' principle as the EC2 instance role.
correct_answers.case_2: Cross-account Role with ExternalId — genuinely external SaaS tools use this pattern, never static access keys.
correct_answers.case_3: Standard EC2 instance role, scoped to sns:Publish on the specific topics needed — same pattern used throughout this whole session.

tasks.explanation: 'service needs access' scenario, trusted entity — Task Role (ECS- instance role- equivalent, per-task scoped), cross-account Role, instance Role. Principle: service assumes a Role, static keys. This is second nature decision.

tasks.scenario: Time to report to Ravi and close this piece.
tasks.question: Write your status update: what was built, and how this session's approach differed from before the investigation.
expected_answer_contains: New EC2 role, Lambda role fix, cross-account CI/CD deploy role with ExternalId, and vendor access role all built and scoped correctly
A final pattern-check confirmed nothing created this session repeats Vikram's leftover-access pattern
Going forward, new access includes review reminders at natural checkpoints, not just at creation
tasks.explanation: Service Integration Layer resolved — first time session-. This is real progress — investigation-, default habit.

arc_outro: Service Integration Layer: secured — and for the first time this session, cleanly, on the first pass. Ravi notices too. 'No surprises this time. That's new.' Three days to the audit. One layer left — the final seal, the one that makes sure none of this can quietly slip again.
